prompt: In GraphQL, what is a resolver?

options.text: A cache layer that sits in front of the database
A function that fetches the value for one field
The schema file that declares every type and field
A component that turns a GraphQL query into SQL

explanation: The engine calls a resolver for each field in the query to fetch its value. (a) A cache may sit behind a resolver, but it isn't one. (c) The schema declares types; resolvers implement them. (d) GraphQL doesn't translate to SQL; resolvers fetch from whatever source they like.

prompt: What does the ! in `name: String!` mean?

options.text: The field is deprecated and should be avoided
The field is required in mutation inputs only
The field is non-null, so it is never null
The field must always be requested by clients

explanation: ! marks a non-null type: the server promises never to return null for it. (a) Deprecation uses the @deprecated directive. (b) ! applies to output and input types alike, not only mutations. (d) Clients still choose which fields to request; ! says nothing about that.

prompt: Which problem is GraphQL mainly designed to solve?

options.text: Slow database queries behind REST endpoints
Many round trips and unused fields for clients
Hard-to-cache responses for public content
Too many services for a gateway to route

explanation: GraphQL targets under-fetching (many round trips) and over-fetching (unused fields). (a) It doesn't speed up databases; without batching it often adds queries. (c) It makes HTTP caching harder, not easier. (d) Routing many services is a gateway's job.

prompt: What is happening and what is the standard fix?
scenario: A query `{ products(first: 100) { id seller { name } } }` makes the database log show 101 SELECT statements per request.

options.text: The database is short on RAM; add memory so lookups hit cache
N+1: one list query plus one per item; batch with a DataLoader
The query asks for too many fields; split it into two requests
Missing index on sellers.id; add one so each lookup is cheap

explanation: 1 + 100 queries is classic N+1 from per-object resolvers; DataLoader batches the 100 seller lookups into one IN query. (a) More RAM makes each query cheaper but still runs 101. (c) Splitting the request keeps the same per-item pattern. (d) An index speeds each lookup, but you still make 100 of them.

options.text: It caches every query result across all users for minutes
It batches keys from one tick into one query, cached per request
It rewrites nested queries into a single SQL join up front
It runs each resolver in parallel on its own DB connection

explanation: DataLoader collects keys requested in one tick, loads them in one batched query, and memoises results for that request only. (a) Its cache is per request, not shared across users. (c) It doesn't rewrite queries into joins. (d) Running lookups in parallel still makes N queries and uses N connections.

prompt: Why don't CDNs cache GraphQL responses by default?

options.text: GraphQL responses are a binary format CDNs can't read
Queries are POSTs to one URL, so caches can't key them
The GraphQL spec forbids caching of query responses
Responses vary per field, so they're always too large

explanation: HTTP caches key on method and URL; POST to /graphql gives them nothing to key on. (a) Responses are JSON. (c) The spec says nothing against caching; persisted queries over GET cache fine. (d) Response size isn't why CDNs skip them.

prompt: What do persisted queries give you? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smaller requests
Cacheable GET URLs
A query allow-list
Automatic batching

explanation: Hashes replace query text (a), stable GET URLs can be cached by a CDN (b), and unknown queries can be rejected (c). Batching (d) is a separate server concern handled by DataLoader.

prompt: Which defence most directly stops this?
scenario: Your public GraphQL API lets anyone query `user { friends { friends { friends { posts { comments } } } } }`. One anonymous client's queries are taking down the database.

options.text: Require HTTPS and an API key so anonymous clients are identified
Depth limits and query cost analysis that reject costly queries
Add read replicas so the deep queries spread across more servers
Add DataLoader so the nested friend lookups are batched together

explanation: Cost and depth limits stop the query before it runs. (a) Identifying clients helps rate limiting but doesn't cap what one query can do. (c) Replicas only raise a ceiling an attacker can still exceed. (d) Batching cuts query count but the work still grows exponentially with depth.

scenario: A news site serves the same article JSON to millions of anonymous readers. Each article changes a few times a day. There is one client, the website.

options.text: GraphQL, so the single client can change fields freely
REST with cacheable GETs served behind a CDN
WebSockets that push each article to open readers
GraphQL subscriptions for live article updates

explanation: Public, read-heavy, cacheable content is where HTTP caching shines, and with one client GraphQL's flexibility isn't needed. (a) costs you easy CDN caching for little benefit. (c) and (d) are for pushed real-time updates, overkill for content that changes a few times a day.

prompt: Where does GraphQL most often sit in a larger system?

options.text: Inside the database, replacing SQL for apps
At the edge, calling REST or gRPC services
Between services, replacing internal gRPC
In front of the CDN, caching every response

explanation: GraphQL is commonly an aggregation layer for front-end clients, calling REST or gRPC services behind it. (a) GraphQL is not a database and doesn't replace SQL. (c) Internal service calls usually favour gRPC for speed and strict contracts. (d) It sits behind the edge cache, not in front of it, and isn't a cache.
